reading.body:
Khosla Ventures led the first venture capital investment in OpenAI's for-profit entity, committing 50 million dollars in January 2019, establishing an early foothold in AI infrastructure funding.

Vinod Khosla's investment thesis connects two eras of computing. Sun Microsystems, which he co-founded in 1982, built the servers and infrastructure that enabled the internet to scale. Khosla Ventures, founded in 2004, shifted his focus to experimental technologies with broad reach. The OpenAI investment in 2019 arrived before the transformer scaling laws were widely understood and before compute constraints became central to AI progress. This was venture capital betting on an unproven team and approach, not yet bidding up valuations based on power and facilities requirements.

The 50 million dollar investment represented an early bet on AI as a technology domain worthy of dedicated capital, but the data does not cover the subsequent rounds of funding OpenAI raised, the expansion of Khosla Ventures' AI portfolio, or the firm's positioning as the power and grid constraints became binding on the industry. It shows the entry point, not the long-term strategy or returns.

standing.watch: The records show the lawsuits against OpenAI and Anthropic entities as filed, with docket monitoring active and no development recorded yet by this tracker. Dates appear for some of these filings, including Bass v. OpenAI, United States v. OpenAI OpCo, Buist v. Anthropic, Smigelski v. OpenAI OpCo, and Grant v. OpenAI, while others carry no date in the records. Nothing in the records states a pending case, planned listing, or dispute involving Khosla personally. What remains unresolved is how these OpenAI and Anthropic matters develop, given that the records note no further movement.
standing.record: The site's records list two companies for Khosla: Khosla Ventures, which he founded in 2004 in Menlo Park, California, as an investor, and OpenAI, founded in 2015 in San Francisco, in which he invested. His earlier record is Sun Microsystems, which he co-founded in 1982 and served as founding CEO. The lawsuits on the site name OpenAI and Anthropic entities, not Khosla himself, and include TradeSun v. OpenAI OpCo, Bass v. OpenAI, United States v. OpenAI OpCo, Buist v. Anthropic, Jiang v. OpenAI Group, Smigelski v. OpenAI OpCo, Grant v. OpenAI, and Vredenburgh v. OpenAI OpCo. The pattern running through the record is an investor's profile attached to OpenAI's legal exposure rather than to any case naming him.
standing.standing: Vinod Khosla stands in artificial intelligence as the founder of Khosla Ventures, the firm he established in 2004, and as an early backer of OpenAI. The records show that in January 2019 Khosla Ventures led a 50 million dollar investment in OpenAI, becoming the first venture firm to invest in the company. He also held a stake described as approximately 5 percent of OpenAI's for-profit entity following that investment. His position rests on that founding role at Khosla Ventures and on the OpenAI stake, rather than on an operating role at an AI company today.
